prompt.context: Your client is Next Level Gaming (NLG), a start-up in the E-sports and computer gaming industry based in Los Angeles, California. NLG is planning to launch its first game – an online, multiplayer role playing game that is unlike any existing franchise. Being a new player in the industry, NLG's CEO, Bobby Beck, has asked for your help in deciding its business model. The company is considering 3 alternatives: a subscription model where players pay a monthly fee; a retail model where players pay full price at initial purchase, and a free-to-play model where the game is free to play but charges players for in-game merchandise.
prompt.question: How would you advise NLG to proceed?

clarifying_info.q: What is the time frame for this decision?
clarifying_info.a: NLG is looking to launch immediately.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the key competitors in this space?
clarifying_info.a: The online gaming industry is dominated by 3 major players who control 35%, 25%, and 20% share respectively. There is a long tail of smaller gaming companies.
Based on preliminary market research, NLG expects the majority of players to be between the ages of 21 to 40.
NLG is planning to launch its game in the US only.

clarifying_info.q: What platforms will the game be available on?
clarifying_info.a: NLG's game is compatible for both Apple and Windows computers.

clarifying_info.q: What were the R&D costs to develop the game?
clarifying_info.a: NLG spent $10 million USD to develop its first game.

exhibits.title: Revenue Assumptions by Business Model
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the three business models (Subscription, Retail, Free-To-Play) across revenue-side assumptions

exhibits.title: Cost Structure by Business Model
exhibits.shows: A table comparing variable and fixed costs for each of the three business models, including a footnote about Free-To-Play costs

data.Footnote: Per customer costs in the table are for all customers, including non-paying customers. Paying customers incur an additional average variable cost of $10

exhibits.title: Survey Results from Beta Test (n=100)
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing survey responses (scale 1–5, where 5 = most likely) from beta test participants across Subscription, Upfront Purchase, and Free-to-Play models for four questions

framework: Break down profitability for each of the 3 business models: estimate # of players acquired × revenue per player minus fixed and variable costs
Compare absolute profit and profit margins across models to identify best financial performance
Assess qualitative factors: competitive response, customer acquisition cost, and long-term player retention
Explore other revenue streams (merchandising, e-sports tournaments) and long-term growth options
Consider future expansion potential: 2nd generation game, mobile/console platforms, geographies outside US

questions.prompt: What factors would you consider to estimate the number of players NLG can target with its first game? How large is this player base in the US?
questions.guidance: Candidate should segment the US population by age (21–40 target), apply PC/computer gaming penetration, and arrive at a reasonable addressable market. The expected answer is approximately 10 million players. Approach may vary; if the candidate's estimate differs significantly from 10M, pressure-test assumptions.

math.setup: Example approach: US population ~330M; ages 21–40 ~25–30% → ~82M–99M; PC gaming penetration among that group ~12–15% → roughly 10–15M addressable players. Round to 10M.

questions.prompt: What is NLG's expected first-year profitability with each of the 3 pricing models?
questions.guidance: Candidate must correctly apply Exhibits 1 and 2. Key watch-out: for Free-to-Play, variable and acquisition costs apply to ALL 50% market-share players, but the additional $10 variable cost and the $100 in-game revenue apply only to the 30% of those who buy in-game content. The $10M R&D cost is a sunk cost and should NOT be included. Fixed costs ($5M + $7M + $3M = $15M) apply to all models. Strong candidates will also calculate profit margins.

math.setup: Addressable market = 10M players. Apply Exhibit 1 for revenues and Exhibit 2 for costs. Fixed costs: $5M (Product Dev) + $7M (Server) + $3M (Other) = $15M for all models.
steps: SUBSCRIPTION — Revenue: 10M × 10% × $10/month × 12 months = $120M; Variable costs: 10M × 10% × ($50 + $35) = $85M; Fixed costs: $15M; Total costs: $100M; Profit: $120M − $100M = $20M; Margin: 20/120 = 16.67%
RETAIL — Revenue: 10M × 12% × $60 = $72M; Variable costs: 10M × 12% × ($22 + $18) = $48M; Fixed costs: $15M; Total costs: $63M; Profit: $72M − $63M = $9M; Margin: 9/72 = 12.50%

FREE-TO-PLAY — Revenue: 10M × 50% × 30% × $100 = $150M; Variable costs (all players): 10M × 50% × ($13 + $7) = $100M; Additional variable costs (paying players only): 10M × 50% × 30% × $10 = $15M; Fixed costs: $15M; Total costs: $130M; Profit: $150M − $130M = $20M; Margin: 20/150 = 13.33%
math.answer: Subscription: $20M profit (16.67% margin); Retail: $9M profit (12.50% margin); Free-to-Play: $20M profit (13.33% margin). Subscription and Free-to-Play tie on absolute profit but Subscription has the higher margin.

questions.prompt: What non-financial factors would you consider in the subscription vs. free-to-play business models?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates organize brainstorming into mutually-exclusive buckets. Key themes: competitive response (how sticky is the player base if a rival launches a similar game?), growth potential (new platform—mobile/console; new geography—outside US; new game—2nd generation), alternate revenue streams (merchandising, e-sports tournaments contingent on large enough player base), consumer preference changes (migration to mobile, generational taste shifts).

questions.prompt: How does Exhibit 3 (beta test survey) impact your outlook on the 3 different business models?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note: (1) For 'Switch to a new game in same genre?', a LOWER score is better — Upfront Purchase scores highest (4.2), indicating lowest loyalty; Subscription (3.6) and Free-to-Play (1.9) show stronger retention. (2) Subscription and Free-to-Play both show high likelihood to continue playing (4.2 and 4.1) and low likelihood to switch genres. (3) Free-to-Play scores highest on 'Recommend to friends' (4.8), indicating strong word-of-mouth potential. (4) The sample size of n=100 is statistically significant. Candidate should connect these data points to the final recommendation.

brainstorming.prompt: What non-financial factors would you consider in choosing between the subscription and free-to-play business models?

categories.name: Competitive Response
ideas: How sticky is the player base if a rival launches a game in the same genre?
Free-to-play's large player base (50% market share) creates a stronger network moat vs. subscription (10%)
Subscription revenue is more predictable but smaller base is more vulnerable to churn under competitive pressure

categories.name: Growth Potential
ideas: New platform: expand from PC to mobile or console where free-to-play is the dominant monetization model
New geography: expand outside US; free-to-play is the dominant model in many high-growth markets (e.g., Asia)
New game: launch a 2nd generation game and leverage existing player base for cross-promotion

categories.name: Alternate Revenue Streams
ideas: Merchandising (branded apparel, collectibles) is easier to monetize with a large free-to-play audience
E-sports tournaments require a critical mass of players — free-to-play's larger base makes this more viable
Sponsorships and advertising are more attractive the larger and more engaged the player base

categories.name: Consumer Preference Changes
ideas: Risk that players migrate from PC to mobile platforms where free-to-play norms are entrenched
Risk that a new generation of players loses interest in the specific game genre
Subscription loyalty metrics (Exhibit 3) are strong but the absolute subscriber base is smaller

recommendation: Recommend the free-to-play business model: it matches subscription on absolute first-year profit ($20M) while capturing a 5× larger player base (50% vs. 10% market share), providing a stronger competitive moat

The larger base unlocks e-sports tournaments, merchandising, and word-of-mouth growth (Exhibit 3: 4.8/5 on 'recommend to friends'), and aligns with expansion into mobile and international markets where free-to-play dominates
Retail should be ruled out: lowest profit ($9M, 12.5% margin) and beta survey shows the lowest player loyalty and highest likelihood to switch genres
risks: Generating sufficient paying conversion rate (currently assumed at 30%) — if conversion falls, revenue drops sharply
Average revenue per paying player ($100/year) must be sustained through compelling in-game content design
Player fatigue or perception of 'pay-to-win' mechanics could damage the brand and reduce retention
next_steps: Design two in-game purchase tiers: cosmetic ('beautify' characters for aesthetic appeal) and time-saving (expedite levelling) to maximize paying conversion across different player motivations
Run a larger-scale beta test to validate the 30% conversion assumption before full launch
Develop a roadmap for mobile and console ports, and identify priority international markets for year-2 expansion
